title: Seeking by Night, and Solomon's Wedding Procession
summary: Lying on her bed at night, the woman seeks her beloved and does not find him, so she goes out into the city streets, asks the watchmen, and finds him at last. She holds him and brings him to her mother's house, then repeats the charge not to awaken love until the time is right. A procession then comes up from the wilderness: King Solomon's carriage, guarded by sixty warriors, arriving on his wedding day.
story: Chapter 2 ended with the woman's declaration of mutual belonging and her call for her beloved to return. Chapter 3 opens with his absence. The woman's night search is the first of two such scenes in the Song (compare 5:2-8), and it shows the other side of love: longing, anxiety, and the risk of loss. The search ends in finding, and the refrain of 2:7 closes this movement. Then the scene changes abruptly to a royal wedding procession, which many readers take as the beginning of the Song's central section (3:6-5:1), where the wedding and its celebration are pictured. Whether the Song tells a continuous story or gathers separate poems, this chapter moves from searching to celebration.
historical: The procession in verses 6 to 11 is Solomon's. The first half of 1 Kings describes his wealth, his building projects, and his use of cedar and other timber from Lebanon, obtained through his alliance with Hiram king of Tyre (1 Kings 5). The sixty mighty men recall the elite warriors of David's time (2 Samuel 23:8-39). The Old Testament does not describe any particular wedding of Solomon, and he had many wives (1 Kings 11:3), so readers differ over whether this procession depicts a historical event, a literary picture of a royal wedding, or the way the lovers see their own wedding, as if the groom were a king. The crown given by his mother would recall Bathsheba, who secured Solomon's succession to the throne (1 Kings 1), but the Old Testament records no ceremony in which she crowned him.
cultural:
City watchmen patrolled the streets and walls at night, guarding against thieves and enemies; a woman alone in the streets after dark would have drawn attention and risked harm (compare 5:7). The woman's mother's house (verse 4) is striking. Israelite households were usually named after the father, but the phrase mother's house appears in a few places, often connected with love, marriage, and women's concerns: Rebekah runs to her mother's household after meeting Abraham's servant (Genesis 24:28), and Naomi sends her daughters-in-law back to their mothers' houses to find husbands (Ruth 1:8). Here it suggests a safe and intimate place connected with the woman's family.

Ancient weddings in Israel involved processions in which the bridegroom and his friends came to bring the bride to his home, or in which the bride was brought to the groom, often with music, lamps, and celebration (compare Psalm 45 and Matthew 25:1-13). Myrrh and frankincense (verse 6) were expensive imported resins, used in worship and as perfume. The column of smoke may be the incense of the procession or the dust raised by its travel. The word translated carriage in verse 9 (appiryon) appears only here in the Bible and may be a loanword, possibly describing a palanquin, a covered litter carried on poles.
literary: The chapter has two distinct parts. Verses 1 to 5 are a first-person account of a search, built on the repetition of the verbs to seek and to find and the phrase the one I love (literally, the one my soul loves), which appears four times. The scene has a dreamlike quality, beginning on a bed at night, and many readers take it as a dream or a vivid imagining of loss. Verse 5 repeats the refrain of 2:7 exactly. Verses 6 to 11 are a different kind of poem, a description of a procession introduced by the question who is this coming up from the wilderness, which recurs in 8:5. The speaker is unnamed and may be the daughters of Jerusalem, a chorus, or the poet. The lavish detail of the carriage (cedar, silver, gold, purple) and the armed guard build up to the chapter's climax: the king on his wedding day, crowned by his mother, the day of his heart's rejoicing.

outline.t: Seeking and not finding: the night search
The watchmen, and the beloved found
Who is this coming up from the wilderness?
The king crowned on his wedding day

doctrines.note: The chapter moves from longing and search to a wedding day, the day of the king's heart's rejoicing (3:11). Marriage is pictured as a public celebration of love, witnessed by the community, not a private arrangement alone.

Wedding imagery in the Old Testament is closely tied to covenant: a public, binding commitment. The prophets use the same imagery for God's relationship with Israel (Hosea 2:19-20; Jeremiah 2:2), so a wedding procession carries overtones of faithfulness and promise.

words.note: Baqash, to seek. It appears four times in verses 1 and 2. The repetition captures the anxiety of the search: she sought him and did not find him. The same verb is used throughout the Old Testament for seeking God (Deuteronomy 4:29; Psalm 27:8), which is one reason allegorical readers heard in this scene the soul's longing for God.

Nephesh, soul, life, or self. The phrase the one I love is literally the one whom my soul loves, repeated four times in verses 1 to 4. The word conveys that her whole being is involved in her love. In Hebrew thought the nephesh is the living, desiring self, and the phrase says that she loves with all she is.

Appiryon, carriage or palanquin. The word appears only here in the Old Testament and may be borrowed from another language. It seems to describe a portable seat or couch carried by bearers, a mark of royal splendor. The poem dwells on its materials, cedar from Lebanon, silver posts, a gold base, and purple fabric, to show the king's magnificence on his wedding day.

Midbar, wilderness. The procession comes up from the wilderness (verse 6). In the Old Testament the wilderness is the place of Israel's forty years of wandering, where God led his people and made covenant with them. The same phrase recurs in 8:5. Allegorical readers connected the image with Israel's coming up from the wilderness into the promised land; others take it simply as the route of the procession toward Jerusalem.

christ: The New Testament does not quote this chapter, but its themes connect with the Bible's larger story in several ways. Jesus speaks of himself as the bridegroom and of the kingdom as a wedding feast (Matthew 22:1-14; 25:1-13), and Revelation ends with the marriage of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7-9). Christian tradition has read Solomon's procession as a picture of Christ, the Son of David, coming for his bride, and a long line of interpreters has read the night search as the soul seeking Christ. Many readers have noticed the resemblance between this scene and Mary Magdalene seeking Jesus in the garden early on the day of the resurrection, not finding his body, asking where he has been taken, and then finding and clinging to him (John 20:1-17). The Gospel does not refer to the Song, so the resemblance is thematic. It is a fitting one: the longing to find the one the soul loves is answered in the risen Christ.

hard.q: Is the man in the Song King Solomon, and how does that fit with Solomon's many wives?
hard.a: Readers answer this question in several ways. Some take Solomon as the male lover throughout, and the Song as a celebration of one of his marriages, perhaps early in his reign before his many foreign marriages led him astray (1 Kings 11:1-8). Others, following a view first proposed in the eighteenth century and popularized in the nineteenth, see three main characters: the woman, her shepherd lover, and Solomon, who tries to win her for his harem while she remains faithful to the shepherd. A third view, common today, reads Solomon as a literary figure: the lovers picture each other as king and queen, just as they picture each other as shepherd and shepherdess, and the royal procession is the way a wedding feels to those in love. The Song's closing verses (8:11-12) seem to contrast Solomon's wealth with the woman's freely given love, which supports the view that Solomon is not simply the hero. The text does not settle the question, and each view has thoughtful defenders. What is clear is that the Song celebrates a love that is exclusive and faithful, whatever Solomon's own record.

questions: The woman searches for the one her soul loves. Have you known a season of searching for someone or something you could not find? How did it end?
The Song pictures a wedding as a public celebration, witnessed by the community. Why might it matter that love and marriage be celebrated publicly rather than kept private?
Christians have often read this chapter as a picture of seeking God. When have you sought God and felt that you did not find him, and what helped you keep seeking?
